lessons.title: Wave Behaviour and the Wave Equation

before.content_html:
Types of Wave

Waves transfer energy from one place to another without transferring matter. The particles of the medium vibrate about their rest positions but do not travel along with the wave. There are two fundamental categories:

• Transverse waves — the vibrations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer. The wave profile forms crests and troughs. All electromagnetic waves, water surface ripples and waves on a string are transverse.
• Longitudinal waves — the vibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Instead of crests and troughs, these waves have compressions (particles close together) and rarefactions (particles spread apart). Sound is the principal example at GCSE.

A critical distinction: mechanical waves such as sound and water waves require a medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel through. Electromagnetic waves such as light require no medium and can travel through a vacuum.

Key Fact

Waves transfer energy without transferring matter. Transverse: vibrations perpendicular to travel direction (crests and troughs). Longitudinal: vibrations parallel to travel direction (compressions and rarefactions). Sound is mechanical — it needs a medium.

Wave Properties

All waves — transverse and longitudinal — are described using four measurable properties:

• Amplitude — the maximum displacement from the rest position, measured in metres (m). A larger amplitude means more energy carried: louder sound, brighter light.

• Wavelength (\(\lambda\)) — the distance from one point on a wave to the equivalent point on the next wave (e.g. crest to crest), measured in metres.

• Frequency (\(f\)) — the number of complete waves passing a fixed point per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Higher frequency means higher pitch for sound, or higher energy for light.

• Period (\(T\)) — the time taken for one complete wave to pass a fixed point, measured in seconds. Period and frequency are reciprocals of each other: \(T = \frac{1}{f}\). A wave with a frequency of 200 Hz has a period of \(\frac{1}{200} = 0.005\) s.

The Wave Speed Equation

Wave speed, frequency and wavelength are related by the wave equation:

$$v = f \times \lambda$$

where \(v\) is wave speed in m/s, \(f\) is frequency in Hz, and \(\lambda\) is wavelength in m. Rearranging: \(f = \frac{v}{\lambda}\) and \(\lambda = \frac{v}{f}\). This equation applies to all waves — mechanical and electromagnetic alike.

Question: A sound wave travels through air with a frequency of 440 Hz and a wavelength of 0.77 m. Calculate the wave speed.

Step 1 — identify values: \(f = 440\) Hz, \(\lambda = 0.77\) m.

Step 2 — apply equation: \(v = f \times \lambda = 440 \times 0.77 = 339\) m/s.

Step 3 — state units: wave speed = 339 m/s (close to the speed of sound in air at room temperature — a good sense check).

Reflection, Refraction and Diffraction

Waves interact with surfaces and boundaries in three important ways:

• Reflection — a wave bounces back from a surface. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (both measured from the normal). Wave speed, frequency and wavelength do not change.

• Refraction — a wave changes speed when it crosses a boundary between two media (e.g. air into glass). If it hits at an angle, it also changes direction. It bends towards the normal when slowing down and away from the normal when speeding up. Frequency stays the same; wavelength changes.

• Diffraction — a wave spreads out after passing through a gap or around the edge of an obstacle. The effect is greatest when the gap width is similar in size to the wavelength. Wider gaps produce less spreading.

Key Fact

Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection. Refraction: wave changes speed (and direction) at a boundary — bends towards the normal when slowing down. Diffraction: wave spreads through a gap most when gap width ≈ wavelength.

In a ripple tank, a vibrating bar produces plane water waves. A light source above projects the wave pattern onto a screen below. To measure wave speed: use a strobe light to “freeze” the pattern, measure several wavelengths and divide by the number of waves to find \(\lambda\). Note the motor frequency for \(f\). Calculate \(v = f\lambda\).

For investigating wave speed in a stretched string (PAG P11): vary the tension by changing the hanging mass, measure the frequency using a signal generator driving the string, and observe the standing wave pattern to determine wavelength from the node spacing. Increasing tension increases wave speed.

Key variables to control: for the string, keep the length and mass per unit length constant when changing tension. For the ripple tank, keep water depth constant — wave speed in water depends on depth.

The speed of sound in a medium depends on the stiffness and density of the material. Sound travels faster in solids than in liquids, and faster in liquids than in gases, because particles in solids are more tightly bonded and can transmit compressions more rapidly. For example, sound travels at approximately 340 m/s in air but around 1,500 m/s in water and over 5,000 m/s in steel.

lessons.title: Wave Interaction: Reflection, Refraction and Lenses

before.content_html:
Reflection at Plane Surfaces

When a wave strikes a smooth, flat surface, it is reflected. The key rule is that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection — both angles are measured from the normal, which is an imaginary line at right angles to the surface at the point of contact.

The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane. During reflection, the wave speed, frequency and wavelength all remain unchanged — only the direction of travel changes. A plane (flat) mirror forms a virtual image: the image appears to be behind the mirror, is the same size as the object, is the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front, and is laterally inverted (left and right swapped).

Key Fact

Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection (both from the normal). During reflection, wave speed, frequency and wavelength are unchanged. A plane mirror produces a virtual image the same size as and the same distance from the mirror as the object.

Refraction at Boundaries

Refraction occurs when a wave crosses the boundary between two media with different optical densities. The wave changes speed, and if it hits the boundary at an angle (not along the normal), it also changes direction.

The rules of refraction are:
• When a wave passes from a less dense medium into a denser medium (e.g. air into glass), it slows down and bends towards the normal.
• When a wave passes from a denser medium into a less dense medium (e.g. glass into air), it speeds up and bends away from the normal.
• The frequency stays the same at both sides of the boundary. The wavelength changes because \(\lambda = \frac{v}{f}\) and the speed changes.

Different wavelengths of light refract by different amounts when entering glass. Violet light slows more than red light, causing the colours to spread. This is how a prism separates white light into its spectrum.

To draw a refraction ray diagram correctly:

1. Draw the boundary between the two media (e.g. air and glass) as a solid line.
2. Draw the normal at the point of incidence — a dashed line at 90° to the boundary.
3. Draw the incident ray and label the angle of incidence (\(i\)) from the normal.
4. Draw the refracted ray on the other side of the boundary. If the ray enters glass from air, it bends towards the normal; the angle of refraction (\(r\)) is smaller than \(i\).
5. If the ray exits glass into air, it bends away from the normal; \(r > i\).
6. Label both media and indicate the direction of travel with arrows.

Lenses — Converging and Diverging

Lenses work by refracting light at two curved surfaces. There are two types:

A converging lens (convex lens) is thicker in the middle. Parallel rays of light passing through it bend and converge at the focal point on the far side. The distance from the lens centre to the focal point is the focal length.

A diverging lens (concave lens) is thinner in the middle. Parallel rays passing through it spread apart (diverge) and appear to come from a focal point on the same side as the incoming light.

Key Fact

Converging (convex) lens: thicker in the middle; parallel rays meet at the focal point. Diverging (concave) lens: thinner in the middle; parallel rays spread apart, appearing to come from a focal point on the same side as the light source.

To draw a converging-lens ray diagram, use three principal rays from the top of the object:
1. A ray parallel to the principal axis → refracts through the far focal point.
2. A ray through the optical centre of the lens → passes straight through without bending.
3. A ray through the near focal point → refracts to travel parallel to the principal axis.

The image depends on the object’s distance from the lens (measured in multiples of the focal length \(f\)):

Object beyond 2f: the image is real, inverted and diminished (smaller than the object). This is how a camera forms an image on its sensor.

Object at 2f: the image is real, inverted and the same size as the object, formed at 2f on the other side.

Object between f and 2f: the image is real, inverted and magnified (larger than the object). This is how a projector works.

Object closer than f: the refracted rays diverge and do not meet on the far side. When extended back, they appear to come from a point on the same side as the object — a virtual, upright and magnified image. This is how a magnifying glass works.

A real image is formed where light rays actually meet. It can be projected onto a screen. Images formed by converging lenses when the object is beyond the focal point are real.

A virtual image is formed where rays appear to come from when extended backwards — no light actually passes through the image position. It cannot be projected onto a screen. The image in a plane mirror and the magnifying glass image are both virtual. Virtual images are always upright; real images are always inverted (for a single converging lens).

The power of a lens is defined as \(P = \frac{1}{f}\), where \(f\) is the focal length in metres and power \(P\) is measured in dioptres (D). A short focal length means a high-power (strongly converging) lens. For a diverging lens, the focal length is negative, so the power is negative. Opticians prescribe spectacle lenses in dioptres: a \(+2\) D lens has a focal length of 0.5 m; a \(-4\) D lens has a focal length of −0.25 m.

Atomic Structure and Isotopes

Every atom has a nucleus made of protons (positive charge) and neutrons (no charge). Electrons, which carry negative charge, occupy energy levels around the nucleus. The number of protons is the atomic number and defines which element the atom is. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. They have the same atomic number but different mass numbers. Nuclear notation is written as \(^A_Z X\), where \(A\) is the mass number (protons + neutrons) and \(Z\) is the atomic number. For example, carbon-12 (\(^{12}_{6}\text{C}\)) has 6 protons and 6 neutrons; carbon-14 (\(^{14}_{6}\text{C}\)) has 6 protons and 8 neutrons.

Key Fact

Isotopes have the same number of protons (same element) but different numbers of neutrons. Unstable isotopes have nuclei that decay spontaneously, emitting ionising radiation. Radioactive decay is random and cannot be predicted for any individual nucleus.

Types of Ionising Radiation

Unstable nuclei emit three main types of ionising radiation:

• Alpha (\(\alpha\)) particles — a helium nucleus (\(^4_2\text{He}\)): 2 protons + 2 neutrons. Strongly ionising because of their large charge and mass. Weakly penetrating: stopped by a single sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air.
• Beta (\(\beta\)) particles — a high-speed electron produced when a neutron converts into a proton inside the nucleus. Moderately ionising and penetrating. Stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.
• Gamma (\(\gamma\)) rays — high-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus. Weakly ionising but highly penetrating: only significantly reduced by several centimetres of lead or metres of concrete.

Increasing ionising power: \(\gamma\) < \(\beta\) < \(\alpha\). Increasing penetrating power: \(\alpha\) < \(\beta\) < \(\gamma\). There is a trade-off — the more ionising a particle is, the more energy it deposits quickly and the less it penetrates.

In any nuclear equation, the mass numbers and atomic numbers must balance on both sides.

Alpha decay: nucleus loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons. Mass number decreases by 4; atomic number decreases by 2.

$$^{238}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow ^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}$$

Beta decay: a neutron converts to a proton. Mass number unchanged; atomic number increases by 1.

$$^{14}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow ^{14}_{7}\text{N} + ^{0}_{-1}\text{e}$$

Gamma emission: no change to mass number or atomic number. Gamma is often emitted alongside alpha or beta decay as the nucleus releases excess energy.

Key Fact

Alpha decay: mass number −4, atomic number −2. Beta decay: mass number unchanged, atomic number +1. Gamma emission: no change to either. Numbers must balance on both sides of a nuclear equation.

Ionisation and Detecting Radiation

Ionising radiation knocks electrons from atoms, creating ions. This damages living cells by breaking chemical bonds and can mutate DNA, potentially causing cancer. Alpha particles are the most ionising, which is why swallowed or inhaled alpha sources are the most biologically dangerous, even though they are stopped by skin externally.

In the laboratory, a Geiger–Müller (GM) tube connected to a counter detects ionising radiation by measuring the electrical pulses produced when radiation enters the tube. The activity of a radioactive source is measured in becquerels (Bq), where 1 Bq = 1 nuclear decay per second. Always measure and subtract the background count rate (radiation present without the source) before recording results.

Half-Life

Half-life is the time taken for the number of unstable (undecayed) nuclei in a sample to halve — or equivalently for the activity to halve. Radioactive decay is random and spontaneous: you cannot predict when any individual nucleus will decay, but you can predict the average rate of decay for a large sample.

After one half-life, half the original nuclei remain. After two half-lives, a quarter remain. After three, an eighth. For example, if a sample has an initial activity of 800 Bq and its half-life is 3 hours, after 9 hours (3 half-lives): \(800 \rightarrow 400 \rightarrow 200 \rightarrow 100\) Bq.

The fraction of radioactive nuclei remaining after \(n\) half-lives is given by: $$\text{fraction remaining} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$$ For example, after 5 half-lives: \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^5 = \frac{1}{32}\). If the original count rate was 6400 Bq, after 5 half-lives it would be \(6400 \times \frac{1}{32} = 200\) Bq.

Background radiation is always present in the environment. Natural sources include radon gas from rocks (the largest source of exposure in the UK), cosmic rays from space, and radioactive materials in food and building materials. Artificial sources include medical procedures (such as X-rays) and discharges from the nuclear industry, though these contribute a much smaller proportion of the total.

Because background radiation varies from place to place and over time, you must take a background count before any laboratory measurement of a radioactive source, then subtract it from your readings to get the corrected count rate from the source alone.

Contamination and Irradiation

It is essential to distinguish between two different hazards:

Contamination occurs when radioactive material is deposited on or inside a person or object. The source continues to emit radiation in close contact with tissues. This is generally considered more dangerous than irradiation because the exposure is continuous and cannot be stopped by simply moving away. It is removed by washing or decontamination procedures.

Irradiation occurs when a person is exposed to radiation from an external source. The person does not themselves become radioactive. Once the source is removed, the irradiation stops. The risk depends on the type of radiation, dose received and duration of exposure.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Radioactive decay is random and spontaneous. Alpha particles (helium nucleus), beta particles (high-speed electron) and gamma rays (EM radiation) differ in ionising power, penetrating power and how nuclear equations change.
  • Half-life is the time for activity to halve. After \(n\) half-lives, \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\) of the original nuclei remain.
  • Contamination (radioactive material on/in the body) is more dangerous than irradiation (external exposure) because it provides continuous, close-range exposure that cannot be stopped by distance.

before.content_html:
Energy Stores and the Conservation of Energy

The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred between stores. In any closed system, total energy before a process equals total energy after. Energy that seems to ‘disappear’ has been dissipated — spread into less useful thermal energy in the surroundings.

Energy can be stored in different ways: kinetic (moving objects), gravitational potential (objects at height), elastic potential (stretched or compressed objects), chemical (fuels, food, batteries), thermal (hot objects), magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear. Energy transfers between these stores via heating, radiation, electrical current or mechanical work.

Key Fact

Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It transfers between stores — kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, chemical, thermal, magnetic, electrostatic, nuclear. Dissipated energy is wasted as thermal energy in the surroundings.

Work Done

When a force moves an object through a distance, work is done. Work done equals the amount of energy transferred. The equation is:

$$W = F \times d$$

where \(W\) is work done in joules (J), \(F\) is the applied force in newtons (N) and \(d\) is the distance moved in the direction of the force in metres (m). One joule of work is done when a force of 1 N moves an object through 1 m.

Work done on an object equals the energy transferred to it. When you push a box across a rough floor, work is done against friction and energy is transferred to the thermal stores of the box and floor. This is why friction causes objects to warm up during sliding — kinetic energy is continuously converted to thermal energy in the surroundings.

Gravitational Potential Energy

When an object is raised against gravity, energy is stored in its gravitational potential energy (GPE) store:

$$GPE = m \times g \times h$$

where \(m\) is mass in kg, \(g\) is the gravitational field strength (10 N/kg for OCR calculations) and \(h\) is the height gained in metres. For example, lifting a 4 kg book to a shelf 1.5 m high: \(GPE = 4 \times 10 \times 1.5 = 60\) J.

Kinetic Energy

Any moving object has kinetic energy (KE):

$$KE = \frac{1}{2} \times m \times v^2$$

where \(m\) is mass in kg and \(v\) is speed in m/s. Notice that KE depends on \(v^2\) — doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy. This explains why stopping distances increase so sharply at higher speeds: a car at 30 m/s has four times the KE of one at 15 m/s and requires four times the braking distance.

A rollercoaster car of mass 500 kg is raised to a height of 40 m before being released.

Step 1 — GPE at the top: \(GPE = 500 \times 10 \times 40 = 200{,}000\) J = 200 kJ.

Step 2 — KE at the bottom (assuming no friction): by conservation of energy, all GPE converts to KE. \(KE = 200{,}000\) J.

Step 3 — Speed at the bottom: \(200{,}000 = \frac{1}{2} \times 500 \times v^2\) → \(v^2 = \frac{200{,}000 \times 2}{500} = 800\) → \(v = \sqrt{800} \approx 28.3\) m/s.

In practice, friction and air resistance would dissipate some energy as thermal energy, so the actual speed at the bottom would be lower than 28 m/s.

Key Fact

Work done: \(W = F \times d\) (joules). Gravitational PE: \(GPE = m \times g \times h\) (joules). Kinetic energy: \(KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\) (joules). Doubling speed quadruples KE.

Power

Power measures how quickly energy is transferred. The equations are:

$$P = \frac{E}{t} \quad \text{and} \quad P = \frac{W}{t}$$

where \(P\) is power in watts (W), \(E\) or \(W\) is energy transferred or work done in joules (J), and \(t\) is time in seconds (s). One watt equals one joule per second. A device with a higher power rating transfers the same amount of energy in less time — a 2000 W kettle boils water in half the time of a 1000 W kettle.

No energy transfer is perfectly efficient — some energy is always dissipated as thermal energy. Efficiency is calculated as:

$$\text{Efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output energy}}{\text{total input energy}}$$

A result of 0.7 means 70% efficient (30% wasted). For example, a motor that receives 500 J of electrical energy and does 350 J of useful mechanical work: efficiency = \(\frac{350}{500} = 0.70\) = 70%. The remaining 150 J is dissipated as heat and sound.

Engineers reduce waste energy through lubrication (less friction), streamlining (less air resistance), thermal insulation (less heat loss) and using more efficient technologies such as LED lighting instead of traditional incandescent bulbs.

Elastic potential energy is stored when a spring or elastic material is deformed:

$$EPE = \frac{1}{2} \times k \times e^2$$

where \(k\) is the spring constant in N/m and \(e\) is the extension in metres. Like KE, EPE depends on the square of the deformation — doubling the extension stores four times the energy. This equation applies only within the limit of proportionality, where force and extension are directly proportional (Hooke’s Law).

Renewable and Non-Renewable Energy Sources

Every power station or device that generates electricity must draw on an energy source. These sources split into two broad categories. Non-renewable sources — coal, oil, natural gas and nuclear fuel — will eventually run out. Fossil fuels formed over millions of years from ancient organic matter; once burned they are gone. Nuclear fuel (uranium) is extracted from finite ore deposits. Renewable sources are naturally replenished: solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, wave, geothermal and biomass.

Key Fact

Non-renewable sources (fossil fuels and nuclear) will eventually run out. Renewable sources (solar, wind, hydro, tidal, wave, geothermal, biomass) are replenished naturally. Nuclear does not produce CO2 during generation but creates radioactive waste.

Comparing Energy Sources

Each source has distinct advantages and disadvantages that must be weighed against each other:

Fossil fuels release carbon dioxide when burned, contributing to the greenhouse effect and climate change. They also release sulfur dioxide (which causes acid rain) and particulates. Despite this, fossil fuels remain significant because they are reliable, energy-dense and can generate electricity on demand.

Nuclear power produces no CO2 during generation and can run continuously as a baseload source. The drawback is radioactive waste, which remains hazardous for very long periods and requires secure storage. Nuclear stations also carry a small but serious risk of accidents.

Renewable sources produce little or no CO2 during operation, making them essential for reducing carbon emissions. Their main challenges are intermittency (wind and solar depend on weather) and, for some, limited suitable locations (tidal, geothermal).

Solar: no pollution during operation, negligible running costs. Disadvantages: depends on sunlight, large area needed for solar farms, panels are costly to manufacture.

Wind: no fuel cost, no direct emissions. Disadvantages: intermittent, visual impact, noise, potential harm to wildlife.

Hydroelectric: reliable, can respond quickly to changes in demand. Disadvantages: damming rivers floods valleys, displaces communities and disrupts habitats.

Tidal: highly predictable because tides are regular. Disadvantages: expensive infrastructure, limited suitable estuaries, risk to marine ecosystems.

Geothermal: reliable, low emissions, compact land use. Disadvantages: only viable where hot rocks are near the surface, high initial drilling costs.

Biomass: theoretically carbon-neutral (CO2 absorbed during plant growth equals CO2 released during burning). Disadvantages: still produces pollutants, and land used for fuel crops competes with food production.

Calculating Efficiency

No energy transfer is perfectly efficient. Some energy is always wasted — usually as heat or sound. Efficiency tells us how much of the energy input is usefully transferred. The equation is:

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output energy transfer (J)}}{\text{total input energy transfer (J)}}$$

Efficiency has no units and will always be between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%). To express as a percentage, multiply the decimal answer by 100. For example, if a motor receives 500 J of electrical energy and transfers 350 J as useful kinetic energy, its efficiency = \(\frac{350}{500} = 0.70\), or 70%. The remaining 130 J is wasted, mostly as heat in the motor windings.

A wind turbine receives 2400 J of energy from the wind in one second. It transfers 960 J as useful electrical energy. Calculate its efficiency and identify the wasted energy.

Step 1: Write the equation. \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\)

Step 2: Substitute values. \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{960}{2400} = 0.40\)

Step 3: Convert to percentage: \(0.40 \times 100 = 40\%\)

Step 4: Wasted energy = 2400 − 960 = 1440 J, mostly lost as heat due to friction in the bearings and turbulence in the air flow.

Key Fact

Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy. The answer is a decimal between 0 and 1 (multiply by 100 for a percentage). Efficiency can never exceed 1 (100%) because energy cannot be created.

Reducing Wasted Energy

Increasing efficiency means reducing the energy lost to unwanted pathways. Common techniques include:

Lubrication: oil or grease between moving parts reduces friction, so less energy is wasted as heat. Insulation: wrapping pipes, boilers and buildings reduces energy lost as heat to the surroundings. Streamlining: shaping vehicles and turbine blades to reduce air resistance reduces energy lost to turbulence. Better materials: using low-resistance conductors in electric motors reduces resistive heating losses.

Sankey diagrams display energy flows visually. The width of each arrow is proportional to the energy it represents. The main arrow splits into a useful output arrow and one or more wasted energy arrows. A more efficient device has a thicker useful output arrow relative to the total input.

The National Grid transmits electricity at very high voltage and low current. This matters because energy lost in cables depends on the current squared multiplied by resistance (\(P_{\text{lost}} = I^2 R\)). Keeping current low dramatically reduces heating losses along thousands of kilometres of cable.

Step-up transformers at power stations raise voltage to hundreds of thousands of volts for efficient long-distance transmission. Step-down transformers near homes and businesses reduce voltage to safe levels for appliances. Transmission efficiency is therefore very high compared with lower-voltage alternatives.

lessons.title: Physics on the Move: Stopping Distances and Momentum

before.content_html:
Stopping Distance

When a driver sees a hazard and brings a vehicle to rest, the vehicle travels a total distance called the stopping distance. This splits into two parts:

Thinking distance is the distance the vehicle travels during the driver’s reaction time — between seeing the hazard and pressing the brake. Typical human reaction time is roughly 0.2–0.9 seconds. Anything that slows the driver’s reaction increases thinking distance: tiredness, alcohol, drugs and distractions such as mobile phone use all have this effect. Thinking distance is directly proportional to speed — double the speed, double the thinking distance.

Braking distance is the distance travelled after the brakes are applied until the car stops. During braking, kinetic energy is transferred to heat energy in the brakes by friction. Factors that increase braking distance include: higher speed (much more kinetic energy to dissipate), wet or icy roads (less friction between tyres and road), worn tyres (less grip), and worn or poorly maintained brakes (less braking force).

Key Fact

Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Thinking distance is affected by the driver (reaction time). Braking distance is affected by the vehicle and road conditions. At higher speeds, both distances increase — but braking distance increases much more because kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared.

A common error is to assume that alcohol or tiredness affects braking distance. They do not — they slow the driver’s reaction, which increases thinking distance only. Road conditions (wet, icy) and vehicle condition (tyre wear, brake wear) affect braking distance only. Speed affects both.

Momentum

Momentum is a property of all moving objects. It depends on both mass and velocity:

$$p = m \times v$$

where \(p\) = momentum in kg m/s, \(m\) = mass in kg, and \(v\) = velocity in m/s. Momentum is a vector quantity — it has both magnitude and direction. A lorry moving at 15 m/s has far greater momentum than a bicycle moving at the same speed, simply because of its much larger mass.

A car has a mass of 1200 kg and is travelling at 20 m/s. Calculate its momentum.

Step 1: Write the equation. \(p = m \times v\)

Step 2: Substitute. \(p = 1200 \times 20 = 24{,}000 \text{ kg m/s}\)

Step 3: State units. The momentum of the car is 24,000 kg m/s in the direction of travel. If the car brakes to rest, all of this momentum must be transferred (to the brake pads as heat, and to the road via tyre friction).

Conservation of Momentum

The law of conservation of momentum states that the total momentum of a closed system (no external forces) does not change. In any collision or explosion:

$$\text{total momentum before} = \text{total momentum after}$$

This is one of the most powerful laws in physics because it applies to every collision — from subatomic particles to spacecraft docking. If two objects collide and stick together, the combined mass moves at a lower velocity so that momentum is conserved.

A 1000 kg car moving at 12 m/s collides with and sticks to a stationary 500 kg car. What is the velocity of the combined vehicles after the collision?

Step 1: Calculate total momentum before. Car 1: \(p = 1000 \times 12 = 12{,}000\) kg m/s. Car 2 is stationary: \(p = 500 \times 0 = 0\) kg m/s. Total before = 12,000 kg m/s.

Step 2: Apply conservation. Total momentum after = 12,000 kg m/s. Combined mass = 1000 + 500 = 1500 kg.

Step 3: Find velocity. \(v = \frac{p}{m} = \frac{12{,}000}{1500} = 8 \text{ m/s}\) in the original direction of travel.

Key Fact

Conservation of momentum: total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after (in a closed system). \(p = mv\) gives momentum in kg m/s. Momentum is a vector — direction matters.

Safety Features and Large Decelerations

Rapid deceleration is dangerous because the force on the body is large. From Newton’s Second Law, \(F = ma\); large negative acceleration (rapid stopping) means large force on vehicle occupants. Modern vehicles use several design features to reduce injury by extending the time over which momentum changes:

Crumple zones at the front and rear of cars deform gradually in a crash, increasing the time for momentum to change and so reducing the peak force on occupants. Seatbelts stretch slightly, extending the stopping time for the passenger and reducing the peak force compared with hitting a rigid surface. Airbags inflate rapidly and deflate as the occupant hits them, spreading the impact force over a larger area and a longer time.

At Higher Tier, this is formalised using the equation \(F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\), where \(\Delta p\) is the change in momentum and \(\Delta t\) is the time taken. The longer the collision time, the smaller the force for the same change in momentum. This is why crumple zones, seatbelts and airbags all work by extending \(\Delta t\).
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Stopping distance = thinking distance (driver reaction time — affected by drugs, alcohol, tiredness) + braking distance (road and vehicle conditions — affected by speed, tyre wear, road surface).
  • Momentum \(p = mv\) (kg m/s). The law of conservation of momentum states that total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after in a closed system.
  • Safety features (crumple zones, seatbelts, airbags) reduce injury by extending the time for momentum to change, reducing the peak force on occupants.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following factors increases thinking distance?
A) Worn tyres
B) Icy road
C) Tiredness
D) Worn brakes
practice_questions.marks: C) Tiredness [1 mark]. Tiredness slows the driver's reaction time, increasing the distance travelled before braking begins. Worn tyres, icy roads and worn brakes all affect braking distance.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the law of conservation of momentum.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for: the total momentum of a closed system (with no external resultant force) remains constant / total momentum before equals total momentum after a collision or explosion.

practice_questions.text: A student is driving at 30 m/s. Explain why the stopping distance at this speed is much greater than at 15 m/s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that both thinking distance and braking distance increase; thinking distance doubles (proportional to speed); braking distance increases by a factor of four because kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared (KE = ½mv²) and so more energy must be dissipated by the brakes.
Secure: Identifies that both components increase and gives a correct reason for braking distance increasing more than proportionally.
Developing: Correctly identifies that stopping distance increases at higher speed but does not distinguish the two components or explain why braking distance increases more steeply.
Emerging: Simple statement that stopping distance increases at higher speed with no explanation.

practice_questions.text: A trolley of mass 3.0 kg is moving at 4.0 m/s. It collides with and sticks to a stationary trolley of mass 2.0 kg. Calculate the velocity of the combined trolleys after the collision.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Momentum before = 3.0 × 4.0 = 12 kg m/s; stationary trolley momentum = 0; total before = 12 kg m/s. By conservation of momentum, total after = 12 kg m/s. Combined mass = 3.0 + 2.0 = 5.0 kg. v = 12 ÷ 5.0 = 2.4 m/s. Direction stated (same as original direction). Units correct throughout.
Secure: Correct method with a minor arithmetic error; direction or units omitted once.
Developing: Momentum before calculated correctly; conservation step attempted but error in combining masses or rearranging.
Emerging: p = mv recalled but not applied correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a crumple zone reduces the risk of injury to a vehicle occupant in a collision.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Crumple zone deforms during the crash, which increases the time taken for the car to stop; a longer time for the same change in momentum means a smaller force is experienced by the occupant (F = Δp/Δt); this reduces the likelihood of injury.
Secure: States that crumple zone increases collision time and therefore reduces the force.
Developing: States that the crumple zone absorbs energy or makes the collision less severe, without linking to time and force.
Emerging: Simple statement that crumple zones protect passengers with no scientific explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe the key differences between thinking distance and braking distance, including the factors that affect each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear distinction — thinking distance is the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time (before brakes applied); braking distance is the distance from brake application to rest. Factors for thinking distance: alcohol, drugs, tiredness, distractions — all increase reaction time. Factors for braking distance: higher speed (more kinetic energy to dissipate), wet or icy roads, worn tyres, worn brakes. Notes that speed affects both. Scientific vocabulary precise throughout.
Secure: Both terms correctly defined; at least two factors for each; clear distinction maintained.
Developing: Both terms mentioned; some factors given; some confusion between which factors affect which distance.
Emerging: One term correctly described; limited factors; some confusion between the two.

knowledge_checks.q: Stopping distance is made up of two parts. Which two?
A 500 kg object moves at 6 m/s. What is its momentum?
Thinking distance is increased by a driver being under the influence of alcohol because it increases the driver's _____ time.
Match each factor to the distance it affects:

flashcard_questions.q: What is the equation for momentum?
What are the units of momentum?
Which part of stopping distance is affected by driver reaction time?

flashcard_questions.a: Any two of: wet/icy roads, worn tyres, worn brakes, higher speed.
flashcard_questions.q: Name two factors that increase braking distance.

flashcard_questions.a: Total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after, in a closed system.
flashcard_questions.q: State the law of conservation of momentum.
A 2 kg ball moves at 5 m/s. What is its momentum?

flashcard_questions.a: It increases the time for momentum to change, reducing the peak force on occupants.
flashcard_questions.q: How does a crumple zone reduce injury in a crash?

flashcard_questions.a: Kinetic energy ∝ speed squared, so more energy must be dissipated by the brakes.
flashcard_questions.q: Why does braking distance increase much more steeply than thinking distance as speed doubles?
Which safety feature stretches slightly to extend the stopping time for a passenger?

flashcard_questions.a: Thinking distance — alcohol slows reaction time.
flashcard_questions.q: Alcohol affects which component of stopping distance?

flashcard_questions.a: It has both magnitude and direction (it depends on velocity, which is a vector).
flashcard_questions.q: Why is momentum a vector quantity?

lessons.title: Beyond Earth: Solar System, Stars and the Universe

before.exam_tip_html: Questions on the life cycle of stars often award marks for each correct stage in sequence. Remember the fork in the path: sun-sized stars end as white dwarfs, massive stars end as neutron stars or black holes. Always include the supernova stage for massive stars. For red-shift, make clear it is the light that is shifted, not the galaxy itself being displaced. The key examiner expectation: red-shift shows galaxies are receding; the further the galaxy, the greater the red-shift (faster recession). CMBR is Higher Tier but worth knowing as additional supporting evidence.
before.content_html:
Our Solar System

The Sun is a star — a common misconception is to treat the Sun as something fundamentally different from other stars. It is an ordinary medium-sized star, sitting roughly two-thirds of the way from the centre of the Milky Way galaxy. Our solar system consists of the Sun, eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets such as Pluto, asteroids and comets. All objects in the solar system are held in their orbits by the gravitational attraction of the Sun.

The eight planets divide into two groups. The four inner planets — Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars — are small and rocky. The four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — are much larger gas or ice giants. The outer planets orbit further from the Sun and take much longer to complete one orbit: Neptune’s orbital period is about 165 Earth years.

Key Fact

The solar system has eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars (rocky inner planets) and Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (gas/ice outer planets). The Sun is a star — the same type of object as the billions of other stars in the Milky Way galaxy.

Satellite Orbits

Satellites orbit planets because of the gravitational force between the satellite and the planet. The orbit is a balance between the satellite’s tendency to move in a straight line and the inward gravitational pull curving its path. Artificial satellites serve many purposes and are placed in different types of orbit depending on their use.

Geostationary orbit sits approximately 36,000 km above the equator. A satellite here completes one orbit every 24 hours, matching Earth’s rotation, so it always remains above the same point on the surface. This makes geostationary satellites ideal for communications (television, telephone) and weather monitoring because a ground station can maintain a constant link without needing to track the satellite across the sky.

Polar (low Earth) orbit sits much closer to Earth, typically 200–2000 km above the surface. The satellite passes over both poles as Earth rotates beneath it, eventually scanning the entire surface. This type of orbit is used for mapping, environmental monitoring and military reconnaissance. Because the orbit is lower, the satellite moves faster and has a shorter orbital period (around 90–100 minutes).

The Moon is Earth’s natural satellite. Gravity keeps it in orbit in the same way it keeps artificial satellites in place. For a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force needed to continuously change the satellite’s direction without changing its speed. Objects in orbit are in a continuous state of free fall towards the planet, but their forward velocity means they never reach the surface — they ‘fall around’ it instead.

The closer a satellite orbits, the stronger the gravitational field it experiences and the faster it must travel to maintain orbit. The ISS orbits at roughly 400 km altitude and travels at approximately 7.7 km/s. Geostationary satellites at 36,000 km travel at a much lower orbital speed of around 3 km/s.

The Life Cycle of Stars

Stars form from nebulae — vast clouds of gas (mainly hydrogen) and dust. Gravity pulls the material inward. As the cloud contracts, it heats up. When the core reaches a high enough temperature, nuclear fusion begins: hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, releasing enormous amounts of energy. This is the birth of a star, which then enters the main sequence — a long stable phase where the outward pressure from fusion exactly balances the inward pull of gravity. Our Sun has been in its main sequence for around 4.5 billion years and has roughly 5 billion years remaining.

When a star exhausts its hydrogen fuel, its fate depends on its mass:

Sun-sized stars: the core contracts and the outer layers expand, forming a red giant. The outer layers are then gently expelled as a glowing shell of gas called a planetary nebula, leaving the dense core as a white dwarf. The white dwarf has no fusion reactions and gradually cools over billions of years.

Massive stars (many times more massive than the Sun): they expand into a red supergiant and then undergo a violent supernova explosion — one of the most energetic events in the universe. The explosion scatters heavy elements (carbon, oxygen, iron) into space; these elements become part of new nebulae and eventually new stars and planets. The core that remains collapses to form either a neutron star or, if the remnant is massive enough, a black hole.

Key Fact

Sun-sized star: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → white dwarf. Massive star: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole.

Red-Shift and the Expanding Universe

When astronomers observe distant galaxies, they find that the light from almost all of them is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum. This is called red-shift. It happens because the galaxies are moving away from us: as the source of light recedes, the waves are stretched, increasing their wavelength and shifting them towards red.

Two crucial observations link red-shift to the history of the universe. First, all distant galaxies show red-shift — every direction we look, galaxies are moving away. Second, the further away a galaxy is, the greater its red-shift, meaning it is moving away faster. This is exactly what we would expect if the universe has been expanding from a single point in the past.

The Big Bang theory proposes that the universe began from an incredibly hot, dense point and has been expanding ever since. Red-shift is key evidence: if galaxies are all moving apart, running time backwards implies they were once all in the same place.

A second line of evidence is the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) — a faint microwave signal detected uniformly from all directions in space. This is the afterglow of the immense heat of the early universe, now cooled to microwave wavelengths as the universe has expanded and cooled. The CMBR was first detected in the 1960s and is regarded as strong confirmation of the Big Bang model.

The OCR specification uses a Doppler ball demonstration to model red-shift: a ball with a built-in oscillator produces a sound of higher pitch when moving towards you and lower pitch when moving away, analogous to light being blue-shifted (approaching) or red-shifted (receding) galaxies.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct sequence for the life cycle of a star similar in mass to our Sun?
A) Nebula → main sequence → red supergiant → supernova → black hole
B) Nebula → main sequence → red giant → white dwarf
C) Nebula → red giant → main sequence → white dwarf
D) Main sequence → nebula → red giant → neutron star
practice_questions.marks: B) Nebula → main sequence → red giant → white dwarf [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a geostationary orbit and a polar orbit.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each for any two correct points:
• Geostationary orbit is much higher (approximately 36,000 km) than polar orbit (200–2000 km).
• Geostationary satellites have a 24-hour orbital period, matching Earth's rotation, so they stay above the same point; polar satellites orbit every ~90 minutes and pass over the whole Earth.
• Geostationary orbits are used for communications/weather; polar orbits are used for mapping/monitoring.

practice_questions.text: Explain what red-shift tells us about the movement of distant galaxies.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Red-shift is the shift of light from distant galaxies towards longer (redder) wavelengths; this occurs because the galaxies are moving away from us; the greater the red-shift, the faster the galaxy is receding, which is evidence that the universe is expanding.
Secure: States galaxies are moving away and that red-shift is the evidence; links to expanding universe.
Developing: Identifies that light is shifted and galaxies are moving but does not link to expansion or the increasing red-shift with distance.
Emerging: Knows red-shift means galaxies are moving but explanation is vague.

practice_questions.text: Describe the sequence of events that leads to a massive star ending its life as a black hole.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correct full sequence — nebula collapses under gravity, nuclear fusion begins (main sequence), star expands to red supergiant as hydrogen is exhausted, supernova explosion occurs, core collapses to form a black hole. All stages named in order, supernova included.
Secure: All stages present with minor ordering error or one stage omitted.
Developing: Supernova and black hole mentioned but intermediate stages missing or confused with sun-sized star pathway.
Emerging: Black hole identified as endpoint but sequence largely absent.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) is considered strong evidence for the Big Bang theory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: CMBR is a faint microwave signal detected uniformly from all directions in space; it is the remnant heat energy from the early hot, dense universe, now greatly cooled and stretched to microwave wavelengths as the universe has expanded; this is exactly what the Big Bang model predicts, so its detection confirms the model.
Secure: Describes CMBR as remnant heat from the early universe detected from all directions; links to Big Bang prediction.
Developing: States CMBR exists and that it supports the Big Bang but does not explain why (no link to early hot universe or uniform detection).
Emerging: Names CMBR as evidence with no explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of nuclear fusion in maintaining a star's stability during its main sequence phase, and explain what happens when hydrogen fuel runs out.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium releases energy, creating outward radiation pressure that balances the inward gravitational force — this equilibrium keeps the star stable for billions of years. When hydrogen runs out, fusion rate drops, gravity wins and the core contracts while outer layers expand. For a sun-sized star this produces a red giant, which eventually sheds outer layers (planetary nebula) leaving a white dwarf. Accurate scientific vocabulary, clear explanation of force balance.
Secure: Fusion described correctly as energy source; force balance explained; red giant stage and appropriate final stage mentioned.
Developing: Fusion identified as energy source; one or two post-main-sequence stages described but force balance not explained.
Emerging: Stars use fusion for energy; red giant stage mentioned; limited scientific detail.
